title: Borrowing in Practice
story: A doctor reads your chart (&), then writes a prescription (&mut). Different interactions with the same data — XIOM's borrow system maps perfectly to real-world workflows.
why: Most real-world code uses borrowing patterns — reading data for display and writing data for updates. Mastering borrow patterns is essential for idiomatic XIOM.
analogy: Think of your data as a shared document. Viewers (&) can all look at once. Editors (&mut) need exclusive access. The system ensures nobody edits while others view.
try_it: Add another borrow function like fn rename(b: &mut Book, new_title: Str). Call it between reads and verify the scoping works.
tips: Group read operations together, then do writes — this minimizes borrow conflicts
Use descriptive function names: describe, display, print for &; update, modify, set for &mut
If a function only reads, take &. If it modifies, take &mut. If it consumes, take ownership
The compiler is your ally — it tells you exactly where borrow conflicts happen
common_mistakes: Using owned parameters when & would work — owned parameters consume the value
Mixing reads and writes without scoping — use { } blocks to limit borrow duration
Forgetting to use var instead of let for values that need &mut access
